description: Four-panel group of computed flow-stress curves (mechanically a composite of four near-identical plots), each plotting Stress (MPa) versus True strain with "Temperature: 950°C" printed inside the panel. Axes are identical: y from about 55 to 125 MPa with labelled ticks at 60, 75, 90, 105, 120; x from 0 to ~0.9 with ticks every 0.1. A solid line is keyed "Experimental" and a dashed line with open circles is keyed "Simulated (Model 1)" in (a) and (c), "Simulated (Model 2)" in (b) and (d). (a) and (b) are transient strain-rate increase tests, magenta "0.01s⁻¹-0.1s⁻¹(0.2 strain)" and light-blue "0.01s⁻¹-0.1s⁻¹(0.4 strain)", with the second stage starting abruptly at true strain 0.2 and 0.4. (c) and (d) are the reverse tests: "0.1s⁻¹-0.01s⁻¹(0.2 strain)" and "0.1s⁻¹-0.01s⁻¹(0.4 strain)". Black curves labelled 0.01s⁻¹ and a purple dashed curve labelled 0.1s⁻¹ give the constant-strain-rate references. In (a) the Model 1 simulated second-stage stresses for the two εI values settle at nearly the same level; in (b) the 0.4-strain Model 2 curve falls distinctly below the 0.2-strain one, matching experiment. In (c) Model 1 delays the post-step softening; (d) reproduces it more closely.

subfigures.description: Stress-strain curves at 950 °C for transient strain-rate increase 0.01→0.1 s⁻¹ at εI = 0.2 (magenta) and 0.4 (light blue), experimental (solid) vs Simulated (Model 1) (dashed with open circles). Constant-condition references: black 0.01 s⁻¹ (solid experimental, dashed simulated) peaking just below 90 MPa then softening to a minimum near 70 MPa, and a purple dashed 0.1 s⁻¹ curve peaking near the 120 MPa gridline region (peak just above 105 MPa gridline area) around strain 0.3. The Model 1 simulations for the two εI values converge to almost the same steady-state level.

Same layout and same experimental curves as (a) but simulated with Model 2. The magenta/blue simulated second-stage curves (open circles) fall more steeply than in (a), and the 0.4-strain curve descends clearly below the 0.2-strain curve, giving lower steady-state stresses that track the experimental solid curves.

Reverse transient: 0.1→0.01 s⁻¹ at εI = 0.2 (magenta) and 0.4 (light blue), experimental vs Simulated (Model 1). The simulated curves (dashed with circles) drop late after the step at strain 0.2 and 0.4; the experimental solid curves soften earlier and faster, reaching a minimum near the 70-75 MPa gridlines, while the black 0.01 s⁻¹ and purple dashed 0.1 s⁻¹ curves give the constant-condition references.

Same tests as (c) simulated with Model 2. The Model 2 simulated curves fall much faster after the step, closely following the experimental solid curves into the low-stress second stage, in contrast to the delayed softening predicted by Model 1 in (c).

observations.observation: All four panels share the same axes: Stress (MPa) on the y-axis with printed ticks at 60, 75, 90, 105, 120, and True strain on the x-axis from 0 to about 0.9 with ticks every 0.1; the text 'Temperature: 950°C' is printed inside each panel.
Line-style key printed in the lower-left of every panel: solid line = 'Experimental', dashed line with open circles = 'Simulated (Model 1)' in (a) and (c) and 'Simulated (Model 2)' in (b) and (d).

Panel (a) and (b) legends read '0.01s⁻¹-0.1s⁻¹(0.2 strain)' (magenta) and '0.01s⁻¹-0.1s⁻¹(0.4 strain)' (light blue); panels (c) and (d) legends read '0.1s⁻¹-0.01s⁻¹(0.2 strain)' (magenta) and '0.1s⁻¹-0.01s⁻¹(0.4 strain)' (light blue).

In every panel the two-stage curves change abruptly at true strain 0.2 and 0.4, matching the two εI values named in the legend; the black dashed curve labelled 0.01s⁻¹ and the purple dashed curve labelled 0.1s⁻¹ are the constant-strain-rate reference curves.

The constant 0.01 s⁻¹ reference curves (black) peak just below the 90 MPa gridline at about strain 0.15-0.2, then soften to a minimum around the 70 MPa gridline near strain 0.6 and rise again at the end of the test.

In (a) the Model 1 simulated second-stage curves (dashed with open circles) for the 0.2-strain and 0.4-strain tests approach nearly the same steady-state stress, lying between the 90 and 105 MPa gridlines.
In (b) the Model 2 simulated curve for the 0.4-strain test falls clearly below the 0.2-strain simulated curve in the second stage, i.e. a larger softening than predicted by Model 1 in (a).

In (c) the simulated stress decrease after the step at strain 0.2 and 0.4 is visibly delayed relative to the corresponding experimental solid curves, whereas in (d) the Model 2 simulated curves drop promptly and lie close to the experimental curves.

The caption states the tests are at T = 950 °C with first-stage strain rate ε̇I = 0.01 s⁻¹ and second-stage ε̇II = 0.1 s⁻¹ for (a) and (b), and ε̇I = 0.1 s⁻¹ with ε̇II = 0.01 s⁻¹ for (c) and (d), at εI = 0.2 or 0.4.
The caption states that (a) and (c) correspond to the simulation using Model 1 while (b) and (d) correspond to the simulation using Model 2.

The citing text states that Model 1 is the constitutive model that does not modify the saturation stress and t0.5 (from Puchi-Cabrera et al.), while Model 2 uses a modified t0.5 and softening coefficient ks (Eqs. (12) and (18)).

The citing text asserts that under the transiently increased strain rate the larger the strain at which the rate rises, the lower the second-stage peak and steady-state stress, and that Model 1 predicted almost similar steady-state stresses regardless of εI (Fig. 8a) whereas Model 2 produced a more significant steady-state decline (Fig. 8b).
The citing text asserts that after a sudden strain-rate decrease Model 1 showed a remarkable delay in predicting stress softening (Fig. 8c) while Model 2 was more accurate (Fig. 8d).
